stem.en: Two equal beams of sunlight reach the Earth at the same moment, one at the equator and one at 60°N. How do the two lit patches of ground compare?

text.en: The patch at the equator is smaller, so each part of it gets less energy.

feedback.en: The patch size is right, but a smaller patch packs the energy in, so each part gets more.

text.en: The patch at 60°N is smaller, so each part of it gets more energy.

feedback.en: It is the other way round: a slanting beam spreads over a wider patch.

text.en: The two patches are equal, so each part gets the same energy.

feedback.en: Slant changes the patch. At 60°N the beam covers about twice as much ground.

text.en: The patch at the equator is smaller, so each part of it gets more energy.

feedback.en: Yes. The same energy falls on less ground.

explanation.en: A beam that strikes the ground straight on covers a small patch. A slanting beam spreads the same energy over a wider patch, so each part of the ground receives less. This is why insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles.

hints.en: Shine a torch straight down on a table, then tilt it. What happens to the lit patch?
The two beams carry equal energy. Which patch shares it among more ground?
